summary:
The Lower Brule Sioux Tribe calls itself Kul Wicasa Oyate, the Lower People. They are Sicangu Lakota, part of the Tetonwan nation. Long ago the Sicangu divided into the Kul Wicasa and the Heyata Wicasa, the upland people. The name Brule comes from French traders' translation of Sicangu.

Chief Iron Nation led the people through some of their hardest years. He signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which set out the Great Sioux Reservation. A federal agency was set up on the west bank of the Missouri River, across from Crow Creek, and the Lower Brule Reservation took shape there in what are now Lyman and Stanley counties.

The Missouri River dams of the 1950s and 1960s hit the nation twice. Fort Randall Dam's reservoir flooded sheltered bottomland pasture. Big Bend Dam took more land and forced the town of Lower Brule itself to move about a mile west. Between them the two dams put much of the tribe's forests, hunting, fishing and gathering grounds, farmland, and settlements under Lake Francis Case and Lake Sharpe.

Tribal government is based in Lower Brule, which is also home to Lower Brule Community College.
